A water level (waterpas) is a traditional leveling tool that uses a water-filled tube or hose to find perfectly horizontal points across long distances. It relies on the natural physical principle that the surface of a liquid at rest in connected containers always seeks the same height due to gravity.
Here is an interactive simulator to visualize how a waterpas works and how gravity keeps the water level perfectly equal on both sides, regardless of height differences.
AI-generated. Don't enter sensitive personal info.
How a Waterpas Works
A water level consists of a long, clear hose filled with water, with both ends open to the atmosphere.
The Principle: Because the ends are connected by the same body of water, it functions as a communicating vessel. Hydrostatic pressure ensures that the water surface at both ends settles at the exact same horizontal plane.
The Benefit: Unlike a short spirit level, a water level allows you to transfer accurate level lines around corners, over obstacles, or across large rooms (e.g., 10 to 20 meters apart).
How to Use a Water Level (Step-by-Step)
Fill the hose: Use a clear hose and fill it almost completely with clean water. Ensure there are no air bubbles inside, as bubbles disrupt the accuracy.
Hold the ends together: Keep both ends of the hose next to each other. The water lines should align perfectly. Mark this baseline.
Position the first end: Hold one end against your reference height mark on the first wall.
Move the second end: Stretch the hose out to the distant area or wall where you need the new mark. Hold the tube end up against the wall.
Let it settle: Wait for the water to stop moving. Once steady, align the water level at the first end exactly with your reference mark.
Mark the line: The water level at the second end now indicates the exact same horizontal height. Mark it on the second wall.

It sounds like you are exploring an industrial or manufacturing process that combines hydrostatic pressure, electrolysis, and 3D extrusion to create or replicate a carbon-based structure (often referred to as a "carbon copy"). 
This combination of technologies is typically used in advanced manufacturing to produce high-density, high-purity carbon or composite parts. 
How These Systems Work Together
TechnologyRole in the ProcessKey Mechanism
3D ExtrusionShaping the CoreA nozzle extrudes a carbonaceous material, polymer precursor, or carbon nanotube paste layer-by-layer to build a 3D geometry.
ElectrolysisStructural BindingAn electric current passes through the material or an electrolyte solution, causing a chemical reaction that deposits, cures, or cross-links the carbon matrix.
Hydrostatic PressureCompaction & DensityEqual fluid pressure is applied from all sides to eliminate micro-voids, trapping density and ensuring the final 3D part is completely solid and uniform.
Common Applications
  • Carbon Fiber Composites: Extruding alignment-sensitive carbon matrices, which are then compressed hydrostatically to remove air pockets before final curing. 
  • Electrochemical 3D Printing: Depositing conductive carbon or metals out of a liquid solution using a localized electrical charge at the nozzle tip. 
  • Isostatic Pressing: Taking a 3D-extruded carbon green body and using high-pressure fluids to densify it into high-strength graphite or carbon-carbon composites.

htmlChunks:
Based on your earlier query about a waterpas (water level), combining hydrostatic principles with 3D extrusion and electrolysis/carbon processing points directly to an advanced, automated method of fluid leveling or depth tracking used in modern 3D manufacturing. 
Here is how these concepts bridge your previous question to your new parameters: 
The "Hydrostatic Waterpas" in Modern 3D Extrusion
In large-scale industrial 3D printing (such as extruding carbon fiber composites or concrete), maintaining a perfectly level bed over a vast area is critical. Traditional spirit levels fail at this scale. Instead, systems use an automated hydrostatic leveling network—essentially a high-tech waterpas. 
  • Hydrostatic Precision: Open fluid reservoirs are placed at the corners of the 3D printer bed, connected by a network of tubes. Just like the manual waterpas, hydrostatic pressure ensures the liquid surface across all reservoirs sits on the exact same horizontal plane. 
  • Electrolytic/Conductive Sensing: To turn this physical liquid level into digital data for the 3D printer, the system uses an electrical current. By using a conductive liquid (or an electrolyte) and a carbon probe, the system measures electrical resistance or capacitance when the probe touches the liquid surface. 
  • 3D Extrusion Adjustment: The 3D printer's computer reads these precise micro-measurements. If one corner of the bed expands or warps due to the heat of carbon extrusion, the printer instantly micro-adjusts its Z-axis extrusion nozzle to perfectly mirror ("carbon copy") the true hydrostatic level line. 
Interactive Hydrostatic Feedback Loop
This simulator visualizes how an automated 3D extrusion nozzle utilizes hydrostatic fluid levels and electrical contact sensing to maintain a perfect, level layer thickness during extrusion.

Advanced Material Synthesis (An Alternative Interpretation)
If you meant creating actual carbon parts rather than bed leveling, you may be referring to Electrochemical 3D Extrusion (ECAM). In this process:
An un-bonded carbon precursor copy is extruded in 3D.
The part is submerged in an electrolyte bath under hydrostatic pressure to force the liquid into every micro-pore.
Electrolysis is triggered, passing a current through the conductive carbon to chemically bind, densify, or electroplate the structure evenly from all directions.

You are describing circuit painting, a popular method for prototyping and educational electronics where conductive ink—like Bare Conductive Electric Paint—is used to draw circuit traces directly onto paper, plastic, or 3D-printed surfaces instead of using traditional copper wires. 
When you connect these painted traces to a Microcontroller Unit (MCU), like an Arduino, Raspberry Pi Pico, or ESP32, you can turn your painted designs into interactive, touch-sensitive interfaces. 
How Circuit Painting Connects to an MCU
 [ Painted Touch Pad ] --------( Painted Trace )--------> [ MCU Input Pin ]
                                                            (e.g., Arduino)
[ MCU Input Pin ] (e.g., Arduino) ",[[" [ Painted Touch Pad ] --------( Painted Trace )--------> [ MCU Input Pin ] (e.g., Arduino) ",0]]]]-->
  1. The Conductive Ink: Materials like Bare Conductive paint are carbon-based and conductive. While they have a higher resistance than copper wire, they easily carry low-voltage signals over short distances. 
  2. Capacitive Touch Sensing: Most modern MCUs have built-in capacitive touch pins. When you connect a painted trace to one of these pins, the MCU can detect the electrical change (capacitance) that happens when a human finger touches the paint. 
  3. The Connection Interface: To bridge the gap between the painted paper and the MCU pins, developers usually use alligator clips, conductive copper tape, or small metal rivets/through-holes clamped directly onto the dried paint. 
Key Technical Considerations
  • Resistance: Carbon-based conductive paint has a noticeable amount of resistance (Bare Conductive is roughly 55 ohms per square at 50 microns layer thickness). Keep your painted traces wide and short to minimize power loss. 
  • Sealing: Once the paint dries, it remains water-soluble. To protect your circuit from smudging or shorting out from sweaty fingers, it should be sealed with a clear acrylic spray or varnish after it completely dries. 
Here is an interactive playground where you can draw painted circuit traces and test how line thickness and length alter the electrical resistance and capacitive signal reaching an MCU.
